planting.note: Detach rooted plantlets that form along the trailing stolons, or divide an established mat, and pot into shallow, wide containers or hanging baskets in spring or summer so plants fill in before winter's lower light.

directions: This Central American relative of the more common flame violet carries quilted, bronze-green leaves on wiry trailing stems and is prized for its clusters of soft lilac-blue flowers rather than foliage color. Grow in bright, indirect to shaded light well away from direct sun, in a loose, peaty, well-drained mix kept evenly moist but never waterlogged. Steady warmth and high humidity encourage the heaviest bloom and the fastest spread of new stolons, which root readily wherever they touch moist soil. It excels in a hanging basket or as a flowering groundcover in a large, humid terrarium, and overcrowded mats are easily thinned and restarted from the rooted runners.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings in a moist, peaty mix in spring or early summer, then move rooted cuttings into a hanging basket once new growth appears so plants establish before winter's shorter days.

directions: Native to Central American cloud forests, this epiphytic trailer carries small, densely hairy leaves on long pendant stems that burst into hooded, orange-red tubular flowers in the typical goldfish-plant shape. Give it bright, filtered light such as an east or shaded south window, since the fuzzy foliage scorches easily in direct sun, and pot in an airy, fast-draining epiphyte mix that mimics its treetop origins. Keep the growing medium barely moist and let it dry slightly between waterings, since the hairy leaves are prone to rot if kept constantly wet, and provide high humidity to encourage continuous flowering. Grown almost exclusively in hanging baskets, it benefits from a light trim after each bloom flush to keep the trailing stems full rather than bare at the base.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem cuttings in a moist, light mix in spring, then pot rooted cuttings into a hanging basket or mounted slab once established so the trailing stems have a full season to lengthen before flowering.

directions: Native to the rainforests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, this large epiphytic trailer produces thick, waxy leaves and showstopping terminal clusters of long tubular flowers that open orange-yellow to orange-red with a blotched red throat. Grow in bright, filtered light such as a sheer-curtained south window, since full sun scorches the fleshy foliage while deep shade suppresses bloom. Use a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix, water thoroughly and then let the top layer dry before watering again, and provide warmth and high humidity year-round since this species resents cool, dry air more than most lipstick plants. It is best displayed in a hanging basket or on a mossy slab where the pendant flowering stems can cascade freely.

planting.note: Propagate by leaf cuttings laid on moist propagating mix or by dividing offset rosettes in spring; this limestone-dwelling species is forgiving and roots readily compared to many woodland gesneriads.

directions: Native to limestone cliffs and caves in southern China and Vietnam, this compact rosette gesneriad (long grown as Chirita eburnea) has thick, softly felted gray-green leaves and sends up slender stalks of small white to pale cream tubular flowers. Grow in shaded to bright-indirect light with no direct sun, in a very lean, fast-draining mix, since its limestone-cliff origin makes it unusually tolerant of brief drying out between waterings compared to most African violet relatives. Average household humidity suits it well, making it one of the easier terrestrial gesneriads for a windowsill or under lights. Remove spent leaves and flower stalks at the base to keep the tight rosette tidy and encourage repeat bloom.

planting.note: Start dormant tubers in pots indoors in late winter and move outdoors after the last frost, or plant tubers directly 1-2 inches deep once soil has warmed; the species dies back to its tuber each winter and resprouts in late spring.

directions: Unlike its showier florist's-gloxinia cousin, this South American grassland species forms a tough, woody tuber that can survive outdoors well beyond typical houseplant hardiness, sending up tall, softly hairy stems topped with clusters of narrow red-orange tubular flowers from midsummer into fall. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled or partial shade, where it pairs naturally with ferns and hostas at the back of a woodland border. Water regularly through the growing season but withhold water once the foliage yellows and collapses in fall, since the dormant tuber is prone to rot if kept wet over winter; in colder zones lift tubers or protect with a thick mulch. It can also be grown as a large container specimen and overwintered dry in its pot in a cool, frost-free spot.

planting.note: Propagate by leaf cuttings or by dividing offset rosettes in spring; young plants are slow to establish but become easy, fast multipliers once rooted.

directions: Discovered on shaded limestone in the Tam Dao region of Vietnam and long sold under the older name Chirita tamiana, this miniature rosette gesneriad has earned its nickname from the metallic silver sheen that overlays its dark green, veined leaves. Short stalks carry small pale lavender-blue flowers with a darker throat above the foliage for much of the year when light is adequate. Grow in shaded to bright-indirect light in a light, fast-draining mix, water from below or around the rosette to avoid wetting the leaf hairs, and keep humidity moderate to high. Its small size and tolerance of average windowsill or terrarium conditions have made it a favorite starter species among gesneriad hobbyists.
